subtype: Being a minority in a group [Receiver]
passage:
Yogesh was the only man on the six-person design team, and by his second month he felt watched. When he made a mistake, he felt it counted for all men. When a client asked, “What does the male perspective say?” everyone turned to him. He over-prepared and stayed silent in meetings.
Deepak, the team lead, noticed. After the client call, Deepak said, “That question wasn’t fair to you. From now on we rotate who speaks to the client, and I’ll say whose work it is.”
The next week Deepak named Yogesh’s layout in front of everyone. Yogesh kept his eyes on the screen, but his shoulders dropped.

qa.q: How many people are on the design team?
qa.a: There are six people on the design team.

qa.q: How did Yogesh probably feel when the client asked about the male perspective?
qa.a: Yogesh was probably uncomfortable and resentful at being asked to speak for a whole group. Over-preparing and staying silent suggest he felt watched and cautious.

qa.q: What did Deepak do that helped Yogesh?
qa.a: Deepak recognised the unfair question, set up a rotation for speaking to clients and credited Yogesh's work by name. Fair treatment took deliberate effort.

qa.q: How might the other team members have felt seeing Deepak change how they worked?
qa.a: They may have felt surprised or thoughtful, seeing that Yogesh had been under pressure. The passage does not say.

grounding: Shows a person who is the only one of their gender on a team feeling watched and speaking for a whole group, and a lead making fairness deliberate.

subtype: Being a minority in a group [Receiver]
passage:
In the site cabin, the foreman laughed. “Keerthana, you’ll want to sit near the door in case the dust bothers you.”
“It doesn’t,” said Keerthana. She was the only woman engineer on the team of nine, and she had checked the drawings three times before the meeting. Her jaw was tight.
Samir, the project manager, put down his coffee. “Let’s start with the report. Keerthana wrote it.”
Afterwards Keerthana said, “I’m not here to speak for all women.”
“Noted,” said Samir. “I’ll rotate the site walks and put names on every report. Tell me if anything slips.”
Keerthana nodded but said nothing.

qa.q: How many people are on the team in the site cabin?
qa.a: The team has nine people.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she said she was not there to speak for all women?
qa.a: Keerthana was probably tired and a little resentful at being treated as a representative rather than an engineer. Checking the drawings three times and her tight jaw show the pressure she felt.

qa.q: What did Samir do to make treatment fairer?
qa.a: Samir began the meeting with Keerthana's report, promised to rotate the site walks and to put names on every report. He also asked to be told if anything slipped.

qa.q: How might the foreman have seen the remark?
qa.a: The foreman probably thought the remark was polite or funny and may not have noticed how it sounded. The passage shows only the laugh.

grounding: Shows the only woman in a team feeling watched and treated as a representative, and a manager making fairness conscious.

subtype: Being a minority in a group [Receiver]
passage: Tenzin was the only person from the Northeast in the thirty-person Pune office, and the product launch was five days away. During the crunch, his manager Jagdish kept making small comments: 'Tenzin, you'll handle the China client, na?' though Tenzin was from Sikkim and spoke no Chinese. At lunch, colleagues asked if he ate 'dogs and all'. They laughed; he laughed too, then stopped eating. He started staying until midnight, fixing every bug himself, feeling that if he failed, people would say 'those people' can't handle pressure. On the fourth night, his colleague Rukmini stayed back too. 'You don't have to prove anything for anyone else,' she said. The next morning she spoke to Jagdish privately, and at stand-up Jagdish apologised for the China comment.

qa.q: Where is Tenzin from?
qa.a: Sikkim.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin start staying until midnight?
qa.a: He felt watched and pressured, afraid that if he failed people would judge everyone from his region.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do that helped, and what else could the team do?
qa.a: She reassured Tenzin and spoke privately to Jagdish, who apologised; the team could also stop the jokes about food and region and share the workload fairly.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have seen the China comment before Rukmini spoke?
qa.a: Probably as a harmless joke, not noticing how it singled Tenzin out.

grounding: The only person from his region in a team feels watched and over-performs, and fairness needs conscious effort from others.

subtype: Being a minority in a group [Receiver]
passage: On the metro construction site in Delhi, Neelam was the only woman among twenty-two engineers. Every mistake she made was discussed at the chai break; every mistake the men made was forgotten by lunch. When a supervisor said, 'Madam, maybe leave the night shifts to the boys,' she took three extra night shifts to prove him wrong. She stopped speaking in meetings unless she was completely sure, afraid of being 'the woman who didn't know'. Her work was excellent. Her voice had almost disappeared. When Payal from HR came for a site visit, she noticed. That evening she asked Neelam, 'How often do you get to lead the review?' 'Never,' Neelam said. The next week Payal set up rotating review leads for the whole team, and Neelam's turn came first.

qa.q: How many engineers were on the site?
qa.a: Twenty-two.

qa.q: Why did Neelam stop speaking in meetings unless completely sure?
qa.a: She felt watched and afraid of being judged as 'the woman who didn't know', as if representing all women.

qa.q: What did Payal change, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Rotating review leads for the whole team, so everyone, including Neelam, gets a turn without having to fight for it.

qa.q: How might the supervisor see his comment about night shifts?
qa.a: He may think he was being protective, not noticing that it singled Neelam out.

grounding: The only woman engineer on a site feels watched, over-performs and goes quiet, until fair treatment is built in.

subtype: Being a minority in a group [Receiver]
passage:
'Farhan, you're coming to the team dinner on Friday?' Nitin asked. 'The tandoori place.'
Farhan hesitated. 'It's Ramzan. I'll be breaking my fast around seven. You go ahead.'
'Oh.' Nitin frowned. 'Why didn't you say anything? You sat through yesterday's lunch meeting not eating.'
'I didn't want to make it a thing.' Farhan shrugged. 'Every time religion comes up, everyone looks at me as if I'm the spokesperson for millions of people.'
Nitin was quiet for a second. 'That sounds exhausting.'
'It is, a bit.'
'Okay. What if we move dinner to seven-thirty? Then everyone eats together.'
'You don't have to—'
'I want to. And no speeches. Just food.'
Farhan laughed. 'Deal. But I'm ordering first.'

qa.q: At what time will Farhan break the fast?
qa.a: Around seven.

qa.q: Why hadn't Farhan said anything about fasting?
qa.a: Farhan felt watched and tired of being treated as a spokesperson for everyone of the same faith.

qa.q: What did Nitin do that showed conscious fairness?
qa.a: Nitin listened, acknowledged the strain, and moved the dinner to seven-thirty so everyone could eat together, without making speeches.

qa.q: How might Nitin's view of Farhan's experience have changed?
qa.a: Nitin realised the quiet pressure Farhan carries as the only one, calling it exhausting.

grounding: The only person of a particular faith in a team stays quiet to avoid being watched, and a colleague makes a conscious, fair adjustment.

subtype: Being a minority in a group [Receiver]
passage: I'm Jagdish, and for my first year at the firm I was the only person on my team who hadn't grown up in a big city. Everyone else had been to the same few colleges. When my Odia accent slipped on a word in a meeting, someone laughed and said, "So cute." After that I was careful with every word. If I made one mistake in a deck, I felt I had proved something about every small-town kid. So I overworked, stayed till eleven, and in meetings mostly said nothing. It was Lavanya, my team lead, who noticed. She began going round the table in turn so nobody had to fight to speak, and once, when a client asked about rural customers, she said, "Jagdish knows this better than any of us." It sounds small. It was the first meeting where I spoke for five minutes straight.

qa.q: How late did Jagdish stay at work?
qa.a: Jagdish stayed till eleven.

qa.q: Why was Jagdish so careful with every word?
qa.a: Jagdish felt watched and anxious, as if one mistake would prove something about every small-town kid.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do that made the team fairer?
qa.a: She went round the table in turn so nobody had to fight to speak, and credited Jagdish's knowledge of rural customers in front of a client.

qa.q: What would change if Lavanya had not noticed?
qa.a: Jagdish might have kept overworking in silence, and the team would have lost that knowledge of rural customers.

grounding: Jagdish recalls being the only small-town member of a team, feeling watched and staying quiet, until a lead made a conscious effort at fairness.
